If you mean the actual root of the phrase, it's unknown, as LSJ mentioned.

What the phrase signifies is craving. It's normally used as drug slang
for withdrawal effects, but can be colloquially used for anything you
really want at the time. Typically used as a verb, i.e. 'I'm jonesing
for a burger, man,' or the like. The verbform is a corruption of the original
Jones, used as a noun (He's got the Jones for some weed/coke/smack).

gomi

Messages.Author: Noal McDonald
Messages.Body:
emmits...@hotmail.com (Emmit Svenson) wrote:
> This may be apocryphal, but I thought "Jonesing" came from a song:
>

> "There's something going on, but you don't know what it is, do

> you, Mr. Jones?" Bob Dylan
>
> "The eagle plucks my eye! The worm, he licks my bones! Feel so
> suicidal, just like Dylan's Mr. Jones! Gonna die! Gonna die!" The
> Beatles

For those that don't know the references, the Dylan song is "Ballad
of a Thin Man" from 1965's "Highway 61 Revisited" album. The chorus
of the song is: "But something is happening and you don't know what

it is, do you, Mr. Jones?"

The Beatle's song is "Yer Blues" from the White Album. The quoted
verse is actually as follows:

The eagle picks my eye
The worm he licks my bone
I feel so suicidal
Just like Dylan's Mr. Jones.
Lonely, wanna die
If I ain't dead already
Ooh girl you know the reason why.

As an aside, the Counting Crows song, "Mr. Jones," is about the
same charcter.

In "No Direction Home," the biography of Bob Dylan written by
Robert Shelton in 1985, there's an applicable quote:

"Mister Jones, one of Dylan's greatest archetypes, is a Philistine,
an observer who does not see, a person who does not reach for the
right questions. He piously pays his social dues through self-serving
tax deductions, pays to watch freak shows but doesn't like the
entertainment, is superficially educated and well bred but not very
smart about the things that count..."

Pretty much your basic poseur. In this case, Mr. Jones pretends to
be a part of the counter-culture, rather than high society, in order
to be considered cool, but really is just faking it and doesn't
care for it much.

Corrections aside, while many of Bob Dyaln's and The Beatles' songs
are about drug use, (i.e., "Mr. Tamborine Man" and "Strawberry Fields")
I don't think that was what Bob Dylan was writing about in this case.

In any event, the word "jones" first saw widespread use in the 1960's
among inner city slang, esp. the black population, to mean the onset
of withdrawal symptoms from heroin addiction. It later came to mean
a carving of any kind. Since Bob Dylan's song was on a 1965 album, it
would have been too late been the origin of the word.

The likely source is probably along the lines of some local guy named
Jones that had a heroin habit that he couldn't afford and continuously
suffered withdrawal symptoms. A phrase gets coined and the usage
spreads and the rest is history.

Oh...and if you find the person responsible for the "Valley Girl Speak"
of the 80's, please kill them by actually gagging them with a spoon.

Regards,
Noal McDonald
VEKN Prince of Metro Detroit

> suffered withdrawal symptoms. A phrase gets coined and the usage
> spreads and the rest is history.

Michael Bradley informs me that "Harry Jones" is listed as a slang
term for Heroin by some online [US] government anti-drug dictionary.

The term, if it was really used, was probably (IMO) a play on the
slang "Mary Jane" used for Marijuana.

At any rate, the term would seem to be the most likely origin of the
current usage of "The Jones". Although, if true, it seems implausible
that Merriam-Webster would be unable to ascertain this origin.

--
LSJ

The dictionary he's thinking of is probably the one run by the Indiana
Prevention Resource Center. It also contains a link to a site run by
the White House. Anyway, if you're interested, the url is:
http://www.drugs.indiana.edu/slang/home.html

None of the dictionaries listed word origins.

> The term, if it was really used, was probably (IMO) a play on the
> slang "Mary Jane" used for Marijuana.

*nods* Quite probably. Besides Harry, I've heard Henry used as well.
(Don't ask where. Suffice it to say that I grew up in a trailer park
in a Detroit suburb that was worse than Detroit itself.)

> At any rate, the term would seem to be the most likely origin of the
> current usage of "The Jones". Although, if true, it seems implausible
> that Merriam-Webster would be unable to ascertain this origin.

That's because Harry, Henry and Jones are usually independent terms
for heroin. Makes sense to combine them. Anyway, after making the
above conjecture, I spoke to my stepfather and he said that Jones (or
Mr. Jones) had been a term for heroin itself before it was used to
mean the withdrawal symptoms. A few web sites back him up, including
this one:
http://www.takeourword.com/Issue040.html

It also has an interesting origin of the word "yen" that I wasn't
aware of.

Regards,
Noal
